notes.front: What does the Scrum Guide mean by calling the Sprint Review a working session?
notes.back: An event where attendees collaborate on what to do next, which the Scrum Team should avoid limiting to a presentation.
notes.explanation: The Guide pairs this with adjusting the Product Backlog to meet new opportunities, so the session can change what happens next.
notes.evidence: Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what to do next. The Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities. The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.
notes.example: Like a tasting in a restaurant kitchen where cooks and regular diners try the new dish together and agree what to change for tomorrow's menu.

notes.front: Why does the EBM Guide include employee attitudes when looking at Current Value?
notes.back: Because employees are ultimately the producers of value.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that engaged employees who can maintain, sustain and enhance the product are among an organisation's most significant assets.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Considering employee attitudes recognizes that employees are ultimately the producers of value. Engaged employees that know how to maintain, sustain and enhance the product are one of the most significant assets of an organization

notes.front: Customers love the product and investors are pleased, but the Developers are exhausted and two have resigned this quarter. The Product Owner is asked whether Current Value is healthy. Which perspective does the EBM Guide say is being missed?
notes.back: A: Employees' happiness, since employees are ultimately the producers of value
notes.choices:
A) Employees' happiness, since employees are ultimately the producers of value
B) None: customer and investor happiness tell the whole story
C) Unrealized Value, since staff turnover is future potential
D) Time-to-Market, since fewer staff will slow releases
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says they do not tell the whole story about the ability to deliver value. C: staff happiness is one of the Guide's Current Value questions, not an Unrealized Value measure. D: the question is about the value delivered today, which the Guide judges partly by employee happiness.
notes.explanation: The Guide says customer and investor happiness do not tell the whole story, and it counts employees as the producers of value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Customer happiness and investor happiness also do not tell the whole story about your ability to deliver value. Considering employee attitudes recognizes that employees are ultimately the producers of value.

notes.front: In the EBM Guide's Current Value example, what is profit one way to measure, and what does it tell you?
notes.back: Investor happiness; it tells you the economic impact of the value you deliver.
notes.explanation: The Guide contrasts this with customer happiness, which says more about where to improve to keep customers.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Current Value (CV)”, p. 9
notes.evidence: While profit, one way to measure investor happiness, will tell you the economic impact of the value that you deliver, knowing whether customers are happy with their purchase will tell you more about where you may need to improve to keep those customers.

notes.front: In the Scrum Guide's short description of Scrum, who inspects the results and adjusts for the next Sprint?
notes.back: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders.
notes.explanation: The Guide builds stakeholders into Scrum's basic loop, so their inspection is part of the framework, not an optional extra.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust for the next Sprint.

notes.front: A Product Owner plans to keep stakeholders away until the product is “finished”, to avoid “noise” about scope. How does this fit the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: D: Badly: the Scrum Team and its stakeholders are meant to inspect the results and adjust every Sprint
notes.choices:
A) Well: stakeholders should only judge the final product
B) Well, as long as the Scrum Master agrees
C) Badly, because stakeholders must attend every Daily Scrum
D) Badly: the Scrum Team and its stakeholders are meant to inspect the results and adjust every Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide's loop has stakeholders inspecting results Sprint by Sprint. B: the Scrum Master cannot waive a part of Scrum's basic loop. C: the Daily Scrum is for the Developers; stakeholders inspect the results, chiefly at the Sprint Review.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes Scrum as a repeating loop in which the Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust for the next Sprint. - Repeat

notes.front: Stakeholders give useful feedback at every Sprint Review, but the Product Owner never changes the Product Backlog afterwards. What is missing?
notes.back: A: Adaptation: the results are inspected but nothing is adjusted for the next Sprint
notes.choices:
A) Adaptation: the results are inspected but nothing is adjusted for the next Sprint
B) Transparency: stakeholders cannot see the Increment
C) A longer Sprint Review, so more feedback can be gathered
D) Nothing: the Product Backlog should stay fixed once written
notes.choicesExplained: B: they do see it and give feedback; the gap comes after inspection. C: more feedback does not help if none of it leads to change. D: the Guide says the Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities.
notes.explanation: The Guide's loop pairs inspecting the results with adjusting for the next Sprint.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust for the next Sprint.

notes.front: According to the Scrum Guide, to whom must the emergent process and work be visible?
notes.back: To those performing the work and to those receiving it.
notes.explanation: Transparency here runs outward as well as inward, so stakeholders receiving the work can see it too.
notes.evidence: The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work.

notes.front: In Scrum, artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that {{c1::diminish value and increase risk}}.
notes.explanation: Important decisions in Scrum rest on the perceived state of its three artifacts, so a poor picture of them misleads those decisions.
notes.evidence: With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

notes.front: A Product Owner keeps the Product Backlog private and shows stakeholders only a polished roadmap slide. Stakeholders are often surprised by what is delivered. What should change?
notes.back: B: Make the work visible to those receiving it too, starting with a Product Backlog they can see and understand
notes.choices:
A) Make the roadmap slide more detailed
B) Make the work visible to those receiving it too, starting with a Product Backlog they can see and understand
C) Share the Product Backlog only with the Developers
D) Send stakeholders fewer updates to reduce confusion
notes.choicesExplained: A: a slide is not the work; the Guide asks for the process and work to be visible. C: the Guide says the work must be visible to those receiving it, not just those doing it. D: less visibility deepens the surprise the stakeholders already feel.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires the process and work to be visible to those receiving the work, such as stakeholders, not only to those doing it.
notes.evidence: The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work.

notes.front: Stakeholders plan a marketing launch from a weekly status report that says “on track”. The Increment itself shows that half the planned work is not Done. What risk does the Scrum Guide point to?
notes.back: D: Decisions based on a low-transparency picture can diminish value and increase risk
notes.choices:
A) None, as long as the status report is sent every week
B) Only that the Developers will be blamed
C) That the launch date must be written into the Definition of Done
D) Decisions based on a low-transparency picture can diminish value and increase risk
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide bases important decisions on the artifacts, not on a report about them. B: the Guide's concern is the quality of decisions, not blame. C: the Definition of Done describes Increment quality, not dates.
notes.explanation: The Guide says important decisions are based on the perceived state of the artifacts, so a misleading picture misleads the launch decision.
notes.evidence: With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

notes.front: At the Sprint Review, a sales lead mentions a new law, effective next quarter, that affects how the product must store customer data. The Product Owner says, “Let's stick to the demo and raise that somewhere else.” What would have been better?
notes.back: C: Discuss it there: changes in the environment are part of the Sprint Review and may lead to adjusting the Product Backlog
notes.choices:
A) Ask the sales lead to raise it with the Developers at the Daily Scrum
B) Note it for the Sprint Retrospective
C) Discuss it there: changes in the environment are part of the Sprint Review and may lead to adjusting the Product Backlog
D) Ignore it until the law is in force
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Retrospective is about quality and effectiveness, not about changes in the market or law. A: the Daily Scrum is the Developers' event for progress toward the Sprint Goal. D: the Guide expects attendees to review what has changed and decide what to do next.
notes.explanation: The Guide says attendees review what has changed in their environment and, based on this, collaborate on what to do next.
notes.evidence: During the event, the Scrum Team and stakeholders review what was accomplished in the Sprint and what has changed in their environment. Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what to do next.

notes.front: The day before the Sprint Review, the main competitor drops its free plan. What should the Product Owner bring to the review?
notes.back: C: Both the Increment and this change in the market, so attendees can decide together what to do next
notes.choices:
A) Only the Increment; market news is for executives
B) Only the market news, cancelling the demonstration of work
C) Both the Increment and this change in the market, so attendees can decide together what to do next
D) A finished decision on the response, for attendees to approve
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide includes what has changed in the environment in the review. B: the review covers what was accomplished as well as what changed. D: attendees are meant to collaborate on what to do next, not rubber-stamp it.
notes.explanation: The review covers both what was accomplished and what has changed, and attendees collaborate on next steps from that information.
notes.evidence: the Scrum Team and stakeholders review what was accomplished in the Sprint and what has changed in their environment. Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what to do next.

notes.front: A supplier's delay puts the Sprint Goal at risk, and a big stakeholder demonstration is planned for the Sprint Review. What does openness call for from the Product Owner?
notes.back: A: Tell the stakeholders about the risk and the challenge now
notes.choices:
A) Tell the stakeholders about the risk and the challenge now
B) Ask the Developers to cut testing so the demonstration looks complete
C) Keep quiet until after the demonstration
D) Present a mock-up as if it were finished work
notes.choicesExplained: C: the Guide says the Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the challenges. B: during the Sprint, quality does not decrease. D: only work that meets the Definition of Done is part of the Increment.
notes.explanation: The Guide names openness about both the work and the challenges as a shared value of the Scrum Team and its stakeholders.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges.

notes.front: An experiment the Product Owner championed did not change customer behaviour at all. The Product Owner is tempted to leave it out of the Sprint Review. What do the Scrum values suggest?
notes.back: A: Share it openly, with what was learned
notes.choices:
A) Share it openly, with what was learned
B) Leave it out, because only successes build trust
C) Report it only to the Scrum Master
D) Relabel it as a success to protect the budget
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says the values, when lived, bring transparency, inspection and adaptation to life, building trust. C: openness in the Guide includes the stakeholders, not only the team. D: that hides a challenge the Guide expects the team and stakeholders to be open about.
notes.explanation: Openness about the work and the challenges is expected of the Scrum Team and its stakeholders alike.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges.

notes.front: Which of the Scrum Master's services to the organisation concerns stakeholders and empiricism?
notes.back: Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists this among the Scrum Master's services to the organisation, alongside removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.
notes.evidence: Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: Several senior stakeholders demand a detailed, fixed twelve-month plan for a highly uncertain product, and the Product Owner is overwhelmed. Who in Scrum can help them understand another way of working?
notes.back: B: The Scrum Master, by helping stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work
notes.choices:
A) The Developers, by estimating every item for the full year
B) The Scrum Master, by helping stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work
C) The stakeholders' own project office, which should take over the Product Backlog
D) Nobody: the Product Owner must deliver the fixed plan
notes.choicesExplained: A: detailed year-long estimates are not how the Guide helps stakeholders with complex work. D: the Guide gives the Scrum Master this service to the organisation. C: the Product Owner stays accountable for the Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach among the Scrum Master's services to the organisation.
notes.evidence: Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work;

notes.front: The head of sales tells the Product Owner, “I outrank you, so my feature goes to the top of the Product Backlog.” What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: B: The head of sales can try to convince the Product Owner, whose ordering decisions the organisation must respect
notes.choices:
A) Rank decides: the Product Owner must reorder
B) The head of sales can try to convince the Product Owner, whose ordering decisions the organisation must respect
C) The Scrum Master decides between them
D) The Developers should vote on the order
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says those wanting to change the Product Backlog do so by trying to convince the Product Owner. C: ordering is the Product Owner's accountability, not the Scrum Master's. D: the Developers select items for a Sprint; they do not order the Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks the whole organisation to respect the Product Owner's decisions, which show in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog.
notes.evidence: For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog

notes.front: A large customer threatens to leave unless their custom report is built next Sprint. Several smaller stakeholders need other items. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: B: Weigh the request against the needs of the other stakeholders the Product Backlog represents, then decide the order
notes.choices:
A) Put it at the top at once, because the customer is large
B) Weigh the request against the needs of the other stakeholders the Product Backlog represents, then decide the order
C) Refuse to discuss it until the next Sprint Review
D) Ask the Developers to add it to the current Sprint regardless of the Sprint Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Product Owner may represent many stakeholders' needs, not just the loudest. C: those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner; the Guide does not make them wait for an event. D: no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: The Guide lets the Product Owner represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog, and the ordering is the Product Owner's decision.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog. Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.
